notes: Case stated on combining community punishment orders; section 51(1) hour limit clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Gibson v Chief Inspector Carroll: consecutive community punishment orders unlawful
key_facts: Justices imposed a community punishment and rehabilitation order for unlawful sexual intercourse requiring 100 hours unpaid work and two years supervision, plus a consecutive community punishment order of 80 hours for disqualified driving.
The combined unpaid work requirement exceeded the 100-hour maximum permitted under section 51(1) for a community punishment and rehabilitation order.
The justices considered section 35(2) permitted consecutive orders because it only prohibited combining separate community rehabilitation and community punishment orders.
Moses J held the consecutive structure could not circumvent the section 51 cap where supervision and unpaid work were both required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates on whether consecutive community punishment orders may lawfully exceed section 51 limits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the combined orders breached section 51(1) and were unlawful; matter remitted to the justices for reconsideration of the disqualified driving offence.
enrichment.ratio: Where a court requires both supervision and unpaid work, the order is a community punishment and rehabilitation order governed by section 51(1); a consecutive community punishment order cannot be used to exceed the 100-hour unpaid work limit, and section 35(2) merely reinforces section 51 rather than permitting circumvention.
legal_issues: Whether consecutive community punishment and community punishment and rehabilitation orders may be combined
Construction of section 35(2) versus section 51(1) of the 2000 Act
Whether the justices' answer to the case stated question should be yes or no
linked_authorities: Gilding v Director of Public Prosecutions CO/816/98

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and disposal are clearly reasoned in a short reserved judgment.

notes: Child bus-stop injury appeal; foreseeability finding upheld on limited documentary evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Chadli v Brooks: no duty on bus driver where child ran to catch bus
key_facts: An 11-year-old boy running along the pavement towards a Routemaster bus stop tripped and his limbs were caught by the slowly moving nearside wheel.
The experienced bus driver Mr Brooks had noticed the boy, was travelling at 2-5 mph and could not have avoided the accident once the fall began.
The claimant argued the driver should have sounded the horn, flashed headlights or stopped short when he saw the boy running near the kerb.
The trial proceeded without oral evidence on agreed facts, photographs and witness statements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal from dismissal of a personal injury claim tried on liability first before HHJ Altman.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to find no foreseeable risk requiring precautionary action by the driver.
enrichment.ratio: A bus driver who sees a child of sufficient age running to catch a bus may reasonably conclude the child is aware of the bus; a remote risk of tripping at the kerb edge in familiar circumstances does not require horn, lights or altered stopping unless the situation plainly calls for reaction.
legal_issues: Whether the bus driver owed a duty to take steps when he saw the claimant running
Whether the risk of the claimant falling into the wheel path was foreseeable
Whether the judge's assessment of kerb and bollard width affected the outcome
linked_authorities: Foskett v Mistry [1984] RTR 1
Armstrong v Cottrell [1992] PILR 109

confidence.notes: Findings on foreseeability and causation are explicit though based on limited documentary evidence.

notes: Commercial resulting trust laches appeal; Frawley v Neill unconscionability principle applied.

enrichment.short_title: Patel v Shah: laches bars dormant investors' resulting trust claims
key_facts: Commercial properties bought at auction in 1989-90 were held in defendants' names while Greetflow Ltd contributed to purchase prices, creating resulting trusts.

After the early 1990s property slump Greetflow failed to pay mortgage shortfalls and was struck off in 1993; its beneficial interest was assigned to the claimants for £1 without notifying the defendants.
The defendants funded shortfalls from their own resources during difficult years; the claimants surfaced in 2002 when properties had recovered value.
The deputy judge dismissed the claims on laches as a one-way bet.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Garnett QC's dismissal of claims to enforce beneficial interests in eight commercial properties and removal of cautions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; laches and unconscionable conduct released the defendants from equitable obligations in respect of capital and income.
enrichment.ratio: In commercial joint ventures to trade land, where investors abandon contributions and risk during loss years but claim capital when values recover, it may be unconscionable to enforce resulting trusts; the Frawley v Neill broad unconscionability approach applies beyond orthodox gift trusts and can defeat claims to trust capital.
legal_issues: Whether laches is available against a beneficiary seeking recovery of admitted trust property
Application of Lord Lindley's partnership laches principle to property joint ventures
Whether unmortgaged properties should be treated differently from mortgaged properties
linked_authorities: Frawley v Neill [2000] CP Rep 20
Mills v Drewitt (1855) 20 Beav 632
Knight v Bowyer (1858) 2 De G & J 421

notes: Section 42 civil proceedings order against persistent litigant; Potter LJ warning noted.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General v Doswell: section 42 civil proceedings order granted
key_facts: Mr Doswell launched 13 unsuccessful actions and applications between November 2000 and October 2003 arising from school injunctions and a 1999 affray conviction.
Proceedings targeted Nottingham City Council, the police, the Home Office and court staff, often pursued by repeated appeals and retaliatory applications.
Potter LJ had warned in September 2004 that Mr Doswell might be a candidate for a civil restraint order.
At the section 42 hearing Mr Doswell again relied on background grievances rather than resisting the order on its merits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for a civil proceedings order under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981.
enrichment.outcome: Section 42 order made; Mr Doswell may not institute proceedings or applications without leave; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant who persistently launches unmeritorious and repetitious proceedings to air grievances against public bodies and court staff, despite repeated judicial rejections and prior warnings, satisfies the criteria for a section 42 civil proceedings order to protect the court and other parties.
legal_issues: Whether the history of proceedings satisfies section 42 criteria
Whether there remains a real danger of further vexatious proceedings
Proper construction of R v Velatza in assessing litigant history
linked_authorities: R v Velatza [1959] 1 WLR 622

notes: Major Hedley Byrne/Caparo actuarial negligence appeal; duty, CFA and reliance fully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Precis v Mercer: no duty of care for due diligence AVR supply
key_facts: Mercer's actuarial valuation report understated Stoves Group's pension deficit at £1.35m rather than £4.5m due to a computational error.
Precis (Glen Dimplex) acquired Stoves relying partly on the AVR supplied during due diligence under a confidentiality agreement excluding agent negligence liability.
Scheme actuary Miss Eyres treated the response as an administrative exercise without reviewing accuracy or assuming responsibility to the bidder.
The trial judge found no duty of care, that Mercer could rely on the CFA exclusion clause, contributory negligence of 25%, but that Precis did rely on the deficit figure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from dismissal of Precis's professional negligence claim and from contributory negligence and reliance findings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; no Hedley Byrne duty assumed; Mercer entitled to CFA exclusion; 25% contributory negligence upheld; reliance finding not disturbed.
enrichment.ratio: Supplying a historic actuarial report during M&A due diligence without review or direct communication does not objectively assume responsibility to the bidder; AVR purpose clauses and arm's-length administrative provision militate against a Hedley Byrne duty, and a private CFA exclusion may be enforced by a third-party agent under the 1999 Act.
legal_issues: Whether Mercer assumed responsibility to Precis under Hedley Byrne/Caparo principles
Whether Mercer could rely on the confidentiality agreement exclusion clause
Whether Precis relied on the pension deficit in fixing its offer price
Whether failure to obtain independent actuarial advice was contributory negligence
linked_authorities: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd [1964] AC 465
Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145
Bank of Credit and Commerce International (Overseas) Ltd v Price Waterhouse [1998] PNLR 564

confidence.notes: Lengthy reserved judgment with explicit dispositions on duty, CFA, reliance and contributory negligence.

notes: Allders administration directions; redundancy payments not administration expenses.

enrichment.short_title: Re Allders: redundancy payments not administration expenses
key_facts: Administrators of Allders Department Stores group companies appointed in January-February 2005 sought directions on treatment of statutory redundancy and unfair dismissal liabilities.
The Insolvency Service contended all statutory employment payments including redundancy were payable as administration expenses under Rule 2.67.
Administrators proposed treating part employee liabilities as preferential under Schedule 6 and the balance as unsecured claims.
Lord Hoffmann's reasoning in Re Toshoku on post-liquidation liabilities was invoked by the Attorney General.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrators' application for directions and a declaration that statutory redundancy and unfair dismissal liabilities are not administration expenses.
enrichment.outcome: Directions given for the Administrators; statutory redundancy and unfair dismissal liabilities are not required to be paid as administration expenses under Rule 2.67 or otherwise.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 99 of Schedule B1 limits priority adoption liabilities to wages or salary and excludes redundancy and unfair dismissal payments; Rule 2.67 does not override that lex specialis, and such statutory employment liabilities are not necessary disbursements within Rule 2.67(1)(f).
legal_issues: Whether redundancy payments are wages or salary under paragraph 99(5)(c)
Whether Rule 2.67(1)(f) treats statutory employment liabilities as necessary disbursements
Application of Re Toshoku to administration expenses
Relationship between Schedule 6 preferential debts and general expense rules
linked_authorities: Re Toshoku Finance UK plc [2002] UKHL 6
Powdrill v Watson [1995] 2 AC 394
Hughes v Secretary of State for Employment EAT/204/94

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis with clear declaratory outcome for administrators.

notes: Section 41 sexual history exclusion appeal; honest belief defence and unsafe conviction test.

enrichment.short_title: R v Bahador: section 41 exclusion of nightclub conduct upheld

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant was convicted of indecent assault after entering a car where the complainant had had intercourse with a co-accused who was acquitted of rape.
The defence was honest belief in consent; the judge excluded cross-examination about alleged stage behaviour at Destiny's nightclub.
The appellant wrongly relied on section 41(3)(b) and (c) rather than section 41(3)(a) because belief in consent is not an issue of consent under section 42.
The appellant had asked his co-accused if the complainant was 'up for it' and made no mention of the stage conduct in his police interview.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on exclusion of complainant sexual behaviour evidence under section 41.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; exclusion of stage conduct evidence was within the judge's discretion and did not render the conviction unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Where the defence is honest belief in consent, section 41(3)(a) applies rather than subsections (b) or (c); even if nightclub conduct is strictly relevant to belief, section 41(2)(b) permits exclusion if refusal of leave would not render the jury's conclusion unsafe, especially where immediate pre-assault conversations were more probative.
legal_issues: Correct subsection of section 41 for honest belief defences
Whether alleged stage sexual behaviour was a relevant issue
Application of section 41(2)(b) unsafe conviction test
Distinction between honest and reasonable belief in consent

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and discretionary reasoning on exclusion are clearly explained.

notes: CFA success fee reduction on near-certain appeal; Brooke LJ strong guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Begum v Klarit: success fees reduced from 70-100% to 15%
key_facts: An appeal against HHJ Kirkham's order was for practical purposes dismissed, with only a minor order in the appellant's favour on limited permission.
Counsel accepted that underlying fact findings meant success on the permitted grounds would be worthless.
Solicitors and counsel had agreed success fees of 70% and 100% respectively on an appeal Chadwick LJ had already limited.
The court applied Cook on Costs guidance linking success fee percentages to prospects of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal summary assessment of costs including CFA success fees on a land sale dispute appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Success fees for both solicitors and counsel reduced to 15% reflecting the minimal litigation risk.
enrichment.ratio: Success fees must reflect realistic prospects; where an appeal is a stone-cold certainty for the respondent after limited permission, agreed success fees of 70-100% discredit the CFA regime and should be reduced to a level matching the small residual risk, here 15%.
legal_issues: Appropriate success fee percentage where appeal prospects are negligible
Application of Cook on Costs risk/prospects correlation
Court of Appeal guidance on additional liabilities in non-RTA litigation
linked_authorities: Atack v Lee [2004] EWCA Civ 1712
Callery v Gray [2002] UKHL 28

notes: Section 423 care home gift and council charges; partial remittal on public law point.

enrichment.short_title: Derbyshire CC v Akrill: section 423 gift and care fee recovery
key_facts: George Akrill gifted his home to his children in November 1997 shortly before entering a nursing home, with leaseback and other estate planning documents.
Derbyshire County Council paid £8,547 in care fees and later reassessed liability using deprivation of capital rules when the deed date was corrected.
Judge Inglis set aside the defendant's defence for non-payment of interlocutory costs but allowed him to appear at trial.
The judge found a substantial purpose of the gift was to put assets beyond reach of future care fee claimants and made section 423 orders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court judgment on council care charges and section 423 claims by council and private care home operators.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part only; section 423 orders upheld; first claimant's debt claim remitted for consideration of public law defence to council reassessment.
enrichment.ratio: A deed of gift before residential care may fall within section 423 where a substantial purpose is protecting the home from future care fee claimants; a litigant debarred for non-payment of costs cannot rely on Article 6, but may raise public law defences to a council's recovery claim under Wandsworth v Winder principles.
legal_issues: Whether section 423 purpose and victim requirements were satisfied
Whether Article 6 was breached by debarring the defendant
Whether public law challenges to council reassessment could be raised in county court proceedings
Application of Regulation 25 deprivation of capital rules
linked_authorities: Wandsworth London Borough Council v Winder [1985] 1 AC 461
Rhondda Cynon Taff County Borough Council v Watkins [2003] EWCA Civ 129
Pawlowski v Dunnington [1999] STC 550

notes: Sierra Leone asylum appeal; adjudicator not obliged to obtain CIPU report of own motion.

enrichment.short_title: Koroma v IAT: adjudicator not required to fetch CIPU report
key_facts: Miss Koroma claimed asylum from Sierra Leone citing RUF-related persecution and Article 3 risks; the adjudicator accepted her account and allowed her appeal.
The adjudicator did not have the April 2003 CIPU country report though other 2003 country material was before him.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal quashed the decision for failure to consult the CIPU report, relying on Ladd v Marshall and E v Secretary of State.
The Secretary of State was unrepresented before the adjudicator due to resource constraints.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal quashing an adjudicator's asylum/human rights decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adjudicator's decision restored; IAT wrongly admitted CIPU evidence and erred in treating non-consultation as error of law; Secretary of State to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator decides on evidence before him and is not obliged to investigate further public-domain country reports of his own motion; absent E paragraph 66 mistake-of-fact unfairness, fresh CIPU material cannot be admitted on appeal merely to challenge factual conclusions and does not establish error of law.
legal_issues: Whether an adjudicator must consult latest CIPU reports in the absence of Home Office representation
Admissibility of fresh country evidence on IAT appeal limited to points of law
Application of Ladd v Marshall and E mistake-of-fact principles
Whether internal relocation to Freetown was reasonably available
linked_authorities: E v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 49
Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489
Owen v Secretary of State for the Home Department IAT 30 July 2002

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of IAT jurisdiction and country evidence rules with clear restoration of adjudicator's decision.
